question: Will I get cut from this process?
context:
I’m interviewing for a Fixed Income Trading Analyst role at Fifth Third Bank in New York. I want you to assess what happened in my most recent interview and what the signals mean.

Background

I currently work at Capital One as a Senior Business Analyst. I went to Cornell and have a 1570 SAT. I’m trying to move into markets/trading.



My Fifth Third process progressed as follows:



Andy Kuhtik — My first conversation in the process. From Andy, I learned more about the seat and that it is not purely an execution role. There is technical/fair-value work involved, including work with structured products and bonds.



Dan — My second conversation. Dan gave me additional context on the role and progression. One thing that stood out was that a junior person can take on a significant amount of responsibility relatively quickly, potentially running much of the process within roughly a year.



Kevin and Jeff — I was then brought in for a 30-minute interview with Kevin and Jeff, who are senior people/desk heads. I viewed getting to this stage as meaningful progression in the process.

The Kevin and Jeff interview

For roughly the first 24 minutes, I thought the interview went extremely well — around a 9/10. The conversation flowed well, I handled the technical and behavioral discussion well, and there seemed to be good rapport.



Around minute 24, they asked some version of:



“Why do you want this job?”



My answer focused mainly on why I want to work in markets. I explained how I became interested in markets and what I find interesting about the work.



Kevin then interrupted me because we were running out of time. This is not something I am trying to interpret as a negative signal. It was clear that the interruption was because there were only a few minutes left in the scheduled 30-minute interview. Kevin used that time to talk more about the role.



After Kevin finished, I asked Jeff one question. Jeff then gave a closing spiel that essentially took us to the end of the interview.

Jeff's closing spiel

This is the part I am actually concerned about.



Jeff talked about the realities of working in the business. He brought up 2008 and said that after the financial crisis there was a period when nobody wanted these jobs. He talked about the nature of the industry, what motivates people to stay in it, and compensation. Among other things, he said that his guys get paid and conveyed that people are there to make money.



Jeff explicitly said that he tells everyone this, which is important evidence that at least some version of this speech is standard.



However, his tone felt harsh and somewhat targeted at me. I don't mean that he literally said, “You're not cut out for this.” He didn't. But the way he delivered the speech gave me a subjective feeling along the lines of:



“Do you actually understand what this business is? Are you sure you're cut out for this?”



That is my interpretation of his tone, not something he explicitly said.



The timing is what makes me particularly unsure how to read it. Immediately beforehand, I had answered “Why do you want this job?” primarily by explaining why markets intellectually interested me. I didn't get into some of my more personal motivations — competitiveness, wanting to work in person, being willing to grind, wanting performance-based upside, etc. Kevin then had to cut my answer short because of time, I asked Jeff one question, and Jeff gave this speech.



The email comment during Jeff's spiel

Jeff also acknowledged that you only get about 30 minutes with someone over Zoom and that it's difficult to fully get to know someone that way.



As part of that discussion, he said we could feel free to send them an email with anything else we wanted them to know.



However, I would not characterize this as a positive signal or a particularly warm invitation to follow up. It was still delivered in the same fairly harsh/blunt tone as the rest of his spiel. He essentially said that they would read whatever we sent but wouldn't reply.



So I don't want the email comment interpreted as “they liked me and wanted to hear more.” It may simply have been part of his standard process: we only have 30 minutes, if there's something else you want us to know, send it; we'll read it, but don't expect a response.



At the same time, it is relevant because it means that sending a substantive follow-up was something Jeff explicitly told candidates they were allowed to do.

Exact sequence

The sequence was:



~24 minutes of what I thought was a 9/10 interview → “Why do you want this job?” → I explain why I want to work in markets → Kevin cuts me off because we're running out of time and talks about the role → I ask Jeff one question → Jeff gives a fairly harsh closing spiel that subjectively feels like “do you understand this business / are you cut out for this?” → Jeff says he tells everyone this → discusses 2008, the realities of the industry, and that his guys get paid → acknowledges that a 30-minute Zoom is limited → says we can email them anything else we want them to know and that they'll read it but won't reply → interview ends.

What I did afterward

Because I thought my “why this job?” answer had been incomplete, I used the opportunity Jeff explicitly gave us and sent the following email later that day:

Hello Kevin and Jeff,

Thank you for taking the time to speak with me earlier today.

I wanted to expand on my answer when you asked why I wanted this job. I said that "I want to work in markets" and explained how I became interested in markets and what I find interesting about the work. What I should have done a better job of explaining is why the environment itself appeals to me and why I am a strong fit for it:

I want to work in person. I go into the office five days a week now, but most days it is fairly empty. I want to work somewhere where the people around me are there every day and I can learn from and interact with them throughout the day.

I am willing to put in the work. We talked about my 1570 SAT score, but I got that score because I took the test three times and kept working at it until I got the result I wanted. The same has been true in school and at Capital One. I have always relied on putting in the hours and being persistent rather than expecting things to come easily.

I am competitive and drawn to the upside. We talked about the success I have had gambling, which is one example of how I have always looked for opportunities to make money. I would bring that same mentality and drive to the desk.

Happy to discuss any of this further. Thank you again for your time.

Best,
Harold

assumptions: The interviewers' harsh tone was a genuine indicator of doubt about cultural/role fit rather than a generic motivational test.
The follow‑up email, while appropriate, will not substantially shift their evaluation given the limited time they allocated for review.
No additional positive signals (e.g., a second‑round interview invitation) have been received since the Zoom call.
Fifth Third’s hiring process typically eliminates candidates after a senior‑level interview if concerns remain about motivation or resilience.
External factors (e.g., hiring freeze, internal candidate pool) are not influencing the decision.
parsed.reasoning: The candidate performed strongly for the majority of the interview, but the pivotal moment—Jeff’s closing remarks—suggested the interviewers were uncertain about the candidate’s true motivation and stamina for a demanding trading environment. Jeff’s explicit invitation to send more information is a routine procedural note, not a positive endorsement. The candidate’s follow‑up email attempts to address perceived gaps, yet such emails rarely overturn a pre‑existing concern, especially when senior leadership has already expressed skepticism. Consequently, the balance of evidence points toward a higher likelihood of being cut from the process.
parsed.key_driver: Jeff's closing spiel that implied doubt about the candidate's understanding of and fit for the high‑pressure trading culture
